subject: WSJ Economics: Health Insurance Is the Sleeper Inflation Issue
body_text:
96 Plus: AI in economics, William Nordhaus’s climate insights, and how the U.S. is beating China in the ‘Global Office’   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Health Insurance Is the Sleeper Inflation Issue   Plus: AI in economics, William Nordhaus’s climate insights, and how the U.S. is beating China in the ‘Global Office’   Food and energy get the spotlight, but there is another source of inflation on the minds of voters headed to the polls today: health insurance.

   At first glance, there ought not to be much to see here. The government’s broadest measure of health inflation was 3% in the third quarter, right in line with its six-year trend.

   Most of people’s healthcare costs are picked up by their employers or the federal government (through Medicare or Medicaid). What consumers see is what those payers pass on: premiums, deductibles, copays and uncovered services.

         According to a survey of employers by KFF, a health research and news organization, average premiums rose 5% this year. This was actually less than employers’ own healthcare costs, which rose 6.4% in the third quarter from a year earlier, the fastest in at least a decade, according to the Labor Department.

   Employers responded to higher costs first by having workers contribute more via deductibles or premiums, cost-sharing for specific services, prior authorization for some services, or changed plans or providers. Contribution increases averaged 16% for individuals and 9% for families, KFF found. (Individuals buying insurance through Obamacare exchanges are coping with steep increases because of a loss of subsidies .) 

   Second, raises became skimpier. Private wages rose just 3.1% in the third quarter from a year earlier, the slowest in five years, the Labor Department reported last week. This may solve a labor-market mystery. Given low unemployment and brisk inflation, why weren’t wages growing faster? Because the money is going to benefits instead. (Guy Berger expands on this in his newsletter .)

         If health prices don’t explain rising employee and employer costs, what does? KFF says it isn’t insurers’ profits or overhead. People may be consuming more healthcare, such as expensive weight-loss drugs. This, though, has yet to show up in faster growth in the volume of health services consumed.

   Whatever the reason, expect this to land in the lap of whichever party emerges victorious.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   An uncomfortable truth about AI’s growing capabilities: The work that many junior white-collar workers have long done will soon be better off automated . So says Harvard’s Jason Furman, who set off a contentious conversation about the future of the economics profession last month when he launched an AI-driven data dashboard, and argued similar tools could replace a significant portion of the junior staff at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, which he previously led. Incubating young talent is important, he acknowledges. But he argues it will be increasingly difficult to justify keeping entry-level staff on board to do tasks a chatbot can accomplish.

   The pioneer of climate economics has died. Yale University’s William Nordhaus was the rare economist who won the Nobel for work of obvious relevance to ordinary people and policymakers. In the debate over global warming, activists highlight the harm from heat-related death, crop failures and the like, while skeptics dwell on the costs of mitigating emissions. Nordhaus, who shared in the 2018 Nobel , made it possible to weigh those competing claims in a single “integrated assessment model” that measured how economic growth affected climate and vice versa. Nordhaus’s model led him to favor a carbon tax to reduce emissions, but not all the way to net zero: The costs weren’t worth it. He died Oct. 30 of brain cancer , age 85, Yale said.

   People who lose their jobs due to AI are having more trouble finding new roles than other displaced workers, Goldman Sachs finds. After an AI-related job loss, workers take about a month longer to find a new job, compared with those who lost work for other reasons, Goldman’s Pierfrancesco Mei estimates. “Younger workers, who are likely more exposed to AI-driven displacement, are navigating this transition better. They are returning to full-time employment faster and cycling through fewer temporary jobs along the way.”

   China has dominated the U.S. in manufacturing for decades. But the U.S. is still winning the knowledge economy . Richard Baldwin of Switzerland’s IMD Business School calculates that China’s manufacturing output climbed by $13.9 trillion between 2008 and 2024, while America’s grew by $2.8 trillion. But during the same period, U.S. output in digital industries— what Baldwin calls “the Global Office” —is up by $7.2 trillion, versus $3.7 trillion in China. Misplaced angst about China’s dominant factories is “manufacturing mesmerization,” in Baldwin’s term: “It’s almost as if it doesn’t count if you can’t drop it on your foot.”

       More From WSJ     Sammy Cossairt, 36, operates cranes in Nashville, Tenn.   • “I’m out in the sun, making my mark on the world,” said crane operator Sammy Cossairt, who makes $120,000 a year. “I think more women would love to get in and make men’s money doing this work, if they only knew.”

   • A Democratic Socialist is campaigning on “pothole politics” in Los Angeles, where it took an average of seven days to fix a pothole in the fiscal year that ended June 30, up from 0.9 days in 2021-22. 

   • Even a midterms sweep today might not hand congressional Democrats the tools they would need to improve how the economy feels to voters because President Trump controls tariffs, war and even a lot of spending, I wrote in my most recent column.

       What to Watch   Tuesday 

   • It is time to elect a Congress. As of Monday evening, prediction markets gave Democrats a 95% probability of flipping the House and a 77% probability of flipping the Senate.

   • In California, voters weigh Proposition 40, a momentous wealth tax that could serve as a blueprint for other states.

   • 10 a.m. ET: The Jolts report from the Labor Department will show how hiring, quits and layoffs evolved in September. In a solid but staid labor market, all three have been suppressed in recent months.

   Wednesday 

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: Economists expect to see the U.S. trade deficit increased to $107.8 billion in September.

   • 8:30 a.m. ET: The Treasury announces its quarterly debt-issuance plans, with investors watching for any changes to issuance of 20- and 30-year bonds.

       Reader Feedback   Thoughts on what you just read? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me.   

   Correction: We misspelled the name of WSJ Economics feedback contributor Jonathan Stekloff as Steckloff.

       What I’m Reading   • A Congressional sweep today would give Democrats a chance to win back voters’ trust on the economy, writes former Biden economic adviser Jared Bernstein : But “if they fail to do so, we’ll be back here again before too long.”

   • A horse partly owned by Fed chairman Kevin Warsh won the $2 million Breeders’ Cup Mile. ( Washington Post )

   • Sports bars are using prediction markets to hedge the risk that customers’ favorite teams get eliminated from the playoffs. ( The Athletic )

   • China’s steel industry is under pressure as costs rise and demand slides. ( Nikkei )

       About Me   I’m The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator. I’ve been writing about economics, markets and politics for more than 40 years, in the U.S. and from around the world.
